newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SOCCER-JAPAN AND SOUTH KOREA ARE WORKING WELL ON WORLD CUP.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-JAPAN AND SOUTH KOREA ARE WORKING WELL ON WORLD CUP.

text.p: Japan and South Korea are working well together as partners in the first co-hosted World Cup in 2002 and have scheduled a second friendly for September in Seoul, FIFA officials said on Tuesday.

"We can report on May 31 to the executive committee of FIFA that the co-hosting of the first World Cup in 2002 between Korea and Japan is really on the right course," FIFA secretary general Joseph Blatter said after a planning group meeting in Zurich.
"We do not see any problems from now to 2002," he said.

Ken Naganuma, head of Japan's national football association, said the Asian countries had agreed to hold another friendly in Seoul on September 17 as the return leg to a match to be played in Tokyo on May 21.
Soccer's governing body also agreed to depart from past practice and let the Asian countries keep all the ticket revenue from matches they host rather than contribute funds to FIFA's pool.
Blatter said FIFA's executive committee still had to approve the proposal, but added he expected no opposition.
The move would set a precedent for future World Cups, he added.
It was triggered by the new financial structure of television revenue and the fact that ticket prices would probably differ in the two countries, he said.
It was still too soon to say how much television revenue the two hosts would receive, he said.

Blatter played down minor differences that emerged at the meeting, such as the lack of agreement over how many mascots to use. FIFA has proposed using one emblem and two mascots, but the idea of three mascots emerged at the meeting, he said.
Even though the first co-hosted World Cup in the event's history is going very well so far, he added, FIFA still considers the arrangement an exceptional one.

South Korea agreed to present its list of stadiums by February 1, 1998. Japan has already presented its list, which exludes Hiroshima, the only potential venue to refuse to build a roof over seats, as required by FIFA rules.
The mayor of Hiroshima is scheduled to visit FIFA on May 18 to argue his city's case, Blatter said.
